doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Playing for the audience with dedication
summary: The player must demand attention with truth and dedication, and audiences cannot be fooled.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: You know let me ask you another thing about jazz. Do you feel that let’s say when a quintet is playing, piano, bass, drums, trumpet, sax, that there are different levels that an audience can listen at?

I think it’s up to the players. Because you could get a quintet and they might not be together. And if the audience listens, they’re not going to enjoy it as much as if they listen to a quintet and the guys are together. It’s up to the players to make the people listen. You demand, the player has to demand attention. Because the audience, they’re hungry man, they want to hear whatever you got to say. So if you say something that’s intelligent and logical and the truth, you got ‘em captivated. But if you go out there caring more about the way you look or what you’re wearing or you know are you playing just to try to get some chick or something, I mean how are you going to—it’s serious. It’s serious business.
In other words how are you going to create something of great beauty if your motive is too weak?

Right. You’ve got to soothe the savage beast in people. So you’ve got to be a dedicated player. People, you can’t fool ‘em. You know you can’t fool people, they’re hungry. And they know the truth now. They’ve listened to jazz for a long time. So you can’t fool ‘em. You know when you’re playing and you play with the blues or you’re playing and you’re just technical playing, you know they know. You can’t fool ‘em now. People will get up and walk out on you. Or they’ll stay there and listen.
